title: AI’s early job signs are good, but ‘only just’ and not for all
full_text:
Early career opportunities are increasing in occupations where artificial intelligence is helping people perform tasks better or faster, but declining where AI is automating work previously done by humans, analysis of millions of job advertisements has found.
The analysis by employment platform SEEK shows the two competing forces of augmentation and automation are shaping the impact of Generative AI (GenAI) on early career hiring across knowledge-based occupations.
The survey found AI was associated with a three percentage point increase in the early career share of job ads for electronics engineers and a 2.7 percentage point increase for civil engineering professionals.
Advertising and marketing professionals recorded a positive net impact of 1.2 percentage points, despite having relatively high exposure to both augmentation and automation.
Software and applications programmers, which had a relatively high automation exposure among the occupations analysed, recorded a 0.3 percentage point decline in the early career share of job ads, while human resource professionals recorded a 0.7 percentage point decline.
SEEK chief economist Blair Chapman said AI might be increasing demand for junior workers in some white-collar roles, particularly where it helped workers complete tasks more effectively rather than replacing them outright. “In other roles, AI appears to reduce demand by doing some tasks itself. This suggests the labour market effects of AI are still unfolding,” he said.
Dr Chapman said the findings supported other research which said after early predictions of a “jobs apocalypse”, AI was “on balance, right now, supporting early career workers in quite a lot of roles”.
“As the report rightly points out, we are only three, four years into this ChatGPT, GPT world and who knows what’s going to happen over the next six to 12 months?” he said. “We are going to update this report annually to get a sense of just how the impact of augmentation versus automation changes over time.” Dr Chapman said the positive impacts were currently outweighing the negative but “only just”.
“I think it makes that early career person a little bit more valuable than they would be,” he said.
“I suppose it shifts them up in value sooner because they can use AI to help get work done a little quicker and their knowledge does not have to be as in depth as it would to do slightly higher value work.” Dr Chapman said members of Gen Z, born between 1997 and 2012, were more likely to be digital natives than their predecessors as they had grown up with the internet, mobile phone, social media platforms and apps.
The most negative impact of AI on a specific job type had been on travel advisers.
In relation to software programmers, Dr Chapman said so much of the role could be automated that “you don’t actually need the junior person, what you actually need is the more senior person to handle the real exceptions”. “Once you have automated all the relatively easy stuff, what you are left with is the more complex stuff where you need knowledge and experience,” he said. “AI can help you with that (but) you are also going to need that human judgment.” Dr Chapman said AI could be used to perform simpler HR functions. “If you are given a list of 100 applications and you want the person with a university degree, AI can check CVs for that so that helps an early career person be more productive,” he said. “It helps the senior person be more productive but the junior person can apply the rules just as easily ...
“So if you had to choose ... you might get an earlier career person because they don’t have as high wage expectations. In this high-cost environment, it’s probably a consideration.” Dr Chapman said capital had always come in and replaced some jobs while augmenting others, citing the agricultural sector shifting from farms using the horse and cart to combine harvesters with smaller workforces.
“We are yet to see (this next wave) be different,” he said.
